name: Electric hairbrush (Victorian)

card.summary: A magnetized 1880s 'electric' hairbrush sold with the promise of a healthier scalp, less dandruff and protection against grey hair and baldness.
card.aka: Electropathic hairbrush; Dr. Scott's Electric Hair Brush
card.note: A historical product; contemporary critics and later historians report it did not generate electric current.

quick.overview:
The Victorian electric hairbrush was a hairbrush sold in the 1880s, best known under the name of George A. Scott, with the claim that a built-in electric or magnetic influence would keep hair and scalp in good condition. Its advertisements promised to treat dandruff and to prevent grey hair and baldness, which is how it was meant to improve a person's appearance.

Its maker presented it as part of a wider fashion for 'medical electricity'. Later accounts describe the internal 'battery' as unable to produce current and the magnet as weak, and the brush shipped with a small compass so buyers could see the needle move.
quick.how: Buyers brushed their hair with it daily, as with any hairbrush; advertisements said the brush's effect came from the handle's electric or magnetic element. Scott also sold related items such as a flesh brush and a toothbrush.
quick.risks: No physical hazard is recorded for the brush itself beyond the ordinary. The documented concerns are about the claims: contemporaries in the electrical press called curative magnetism quackery, and the product's promises were never backed by published tests.

lead: The Victorian electric hairbrush was a late nineteenth-century grooming product marketed as an 'electric' or 'electropathic' brush that would improve the condition of the hair and scalp. It is most associated with George A. Scott, who sold 'Dr. Scott's Electric Hair Brush' in Britain and the United States in the 1880s. [2]

An October 1882 newspaper advertisement described by a London local-history blog said the brush would treat nervous and bilious headaches, neuralgia and dandruff and would prevent grey hair and baldness. The advertisement warned of imitations and gave the shop's address, a few doors from an early public electricity generator in Holborn. [1]

Historical write-ups say the product did not run on electricity: the advertised cell of zinc and copper separated by felt could not generate current, and later versions used a magnet too weak to lift pins, with a compass included so the buyer could watch the needle move. [2] The brush is now discussed mainly as an example of the period's electrotherapy and patent-medicine marketing.

angle.text: Customers used it as their everyday hairbrush, with the promise of a healthier scalp, less dandruff and slower greying or hair loss. The appeal was a better-looking head of hair through a grooming tool they already used.

infobox: Hairbrush marketed as electric or magnetic
Dandruff, headaches, neuralgia, prevention of grey hair and baldness [1]

paras: Scott's advertising relied on testimonials, large claims, money-back offers and criticism of orthodox doctors, according to a Science-Based Medicine account of the period. Because each device was sold for one user, a household was encouraged to buy one for every member. [2]
Scott also sold electric corsets, belts and similar appliances. Accounts differ on whether he held medical training and on his nationality. [2]

sections.h: How the brush was said to work
paras: Advertisements spoke of a continuous electric current. Later commentary describes a zinc plate and a copper plate separated by felt, which it says could not produce electricity, and a magnet in later models too weak to move pins. [2]

A writer in The Electrician condemned curative magnetism as quackery, and the Lancet still carried advertisements for such products, according to the same account. Criticism did not noticeably slow sales of medical-electricity devices. [2]

timeline.event: A London newspaper advertisement for Dr. Scott's Electric Hair Brush lists dandruff, headaches and prevention of grey hair and baldness among its claimed uses. [1]
Scott dies wealthy, per a later account. [2]
